title: Factorisation
tagline: Turning sums back into products, and solving by factorisation

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep. Every identity and numerical check in this chapter was independently reproduced by scripts/verify-math.mjs using exact symbolic and integer arithmetic.

overview.intro: Factorisation is expansion run backwards. Where expansion turns a product into a sum, factorisation turns a sum back into a product, and that reversal is what makes an unsolvable-looking equation solvable. The method for splitting the middle term is the centre of the chapter: given x^2 + 7x + 12, you deliberately split the 7 into 3 + 4 so that the pair 3 and 4 multiplies to 12, and the expression then reorganises itself into a product.

facts.label: Key identities
facts.value: a^2 - b^2, a^3 + b^3, a^3 - b^3, quadratic trinomials

facts.label: Central technique
facts.value: Splitting the middle term into two factors whose product is the constant

blocks.text: Before anything else, look at every term and ask whether they share a factor. This is always safe and always simplifies the work. If every term is divisible by some number, letter or power of a letter, take the lowest common multiple of those out and divide every term by it.

items: x^2 y^3 + x^3 y^2 becomes x^2 y^2(y + x), since x^2 y^2 divides both terms.
Do this first, always. Splitting the middle term before taking out a factor is wasted effort.

blocks.text: The common factor is the least common multiple, not the greatest. Taking a factor larger than the true common factor leaves a fraction, and fractions inside brackets make a later step harder, not easier.

items.note: The common factor is 5x, not 10x, since 15x divided by 10x is not a whole number. Result: 5x(2x - 3).
Common factor is 6a^2 b. Result: 6a^2 b(2a - 3b).

blocks.text: This identity follows from multiplying out (a + b)(a - b): the middle terms cancel because ab - ab = 0, leaving a^2 - b^2. Because the order of subtraction does not change the squares, the same formula works with a and b swapped, so the factorisation is the same either way round.

items: x^4 - y^4 = (x^2 + y^2)(x^2 - y^2), applying the identity twice
For four-term expressions of the form A - B where both A and B are perfect squares, factor twice.
A sum of two squares cannot be factorised this way over the integers.

blocks.text: A term that looks awkward is often a perfect square in disguise. 9x^2 is (3x)^2, 49 is 7^2, and 25x^2 y^2 is (5xy)^2. Reducing each square term to its root before applying the identity is the step most often missed.

items.note: First (x^2 + 9y^2)(x^2 - 9y^2); the second factor is itself (x + 3y)(x - 3y), giving (x^2 + 9y^2)(x + 3y)(x - 3y).

learn.title: The sum and difference of two cubes

blocks.text: The cube identities follow from expansion just as the square identities do. They are worth learning as a pair, because the difference-of-cubes has a minus sign throughout while the sum-of-cubes has a plus and then a minus, which is the detail most often lost.

items: Remember the squares: the expression a^2 - ab + b^2 is often written a^2 + b^2 - ab.
Both factors are needed; leaving out the quadratic factor is the classic error.

blocks.text: Unlike the difference of squares, both a sum and a difference of cubes factorise. That makes this identity useful for simplifying expressions that appear not to factor at all.

learn.title: Factorising quadratic trinomials by splitting the middle term

blocks.text: An expression of the form x^2 + px + q factors only if there are two numbers whose sum is p and whose product is q. When such numbers exist, the method is to rewrite the middle term as their sum, then group the terms so that each group can be taken out in turn.

items: x^2 + 7x + 12: the numbers are 3 and 4, since 3 + 4 = 7 and 3 x 4 = 12.

blocks.text: When the middle coefficient is negative, the two numbers have opposite signs. For x^2 - 7x + 12 the numbers are -3 and -4, since -3 + -4 = -7 and -3 x -4 = 12, giving (x - 3)(x - 4). The constant term's sign tells you the signs of the pair.

Finding the pair is trial and error, but two facts narrow it down. The factors must divide the constant term, and the larger of the two must have the sign of the middle coefficient. Listing factor pairs of q and checking which pair sums to p takes only a moment and eliminates most guesses.

items.note: Pairs of -7: (1,-7) and (-1,7). The pair summing to 6 is (7,-1), giving (x + 7)(x - 1).

learn.title: Grouping, and simplifying a quotient of cubes

blocks.text: Grouping is the general technique: arrange the terms so that a common factor can be taken out of each group in turn, and continue until nothing more can be factored. It is how expressions with four or more terms are handled.

items: xy^2 + 2x^2y + 4 becomes xy(y + 2x + 4) after taking out xy; the bracket does not factor further.
For expressions such as (x^2 + y^3)/(x + y), look for a sum of cubes: x^2 + y^3 is not one, but x^3 + y^3 is, giving (x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2), which cancels to x^2 - xy + y^2.

blocks.text: Simplifying a fraction by cancelling a common algebraic factor is only legal when that factor is a factor of the numerator expression and of the denominator expression. You may not cancel a term inside an addition.

items.note: Using the sum-of-cubes identity the fraction is (x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2)/(x + y) = x^2 - xy + y^2.
Group as a^2(b + 1) - ab(b + 1), then take the common bracket to get a(a - b)(b + 1).

keyPoints: Always take out a common factor first.
The common factor is the lowest common multiple, not the greatest.
a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b), and only a difference factorises this way.
In a quadratic, the split pair must sum to the middle coefficient and multiply to the constant.
The constant term decides the signs: positive constant means both signs agree, negative means they differ.
x^4 - y^4 factorises twice, since x^4 - y^4 = (x^2 + y^2)(x^2 - y^2).
You may cancel a common factor in a fraction but never a term inside an addition.
examFocus: Factorising a quadratic by splitting the middle term is the single most examinable skill in this chapter, usually as a three- or four-mark question.
Always check a quadratic first for a common factor; many exam trinomials have one.
Solving equations by factorisation tests whether you can factorise, so the two topics are examined together.
Simplifying algebraic fractions is common and is lost easily at the cancellation step.

vocabulary.meaning: Rewrite an expression as a product of simpler expressions.
A factor dividing every term of an expression.
An expression of three terms, typically x^2 + px + q.
Reordering terms so a common factor can be taken out of each group.

questions.prompt: Which expression is the factorisation of x^2 - 25?
questions.explanation: x^2 - 25 is the difference of the squares x^2 and 5^2, so a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b) gives (x + 5)(x - 5).
questions.commonMistake: Choosing (x - 5)^2, which expands to x^2 - 10x + 25.

questions.prompt: The common factor taken out of 10x^2 - 15x is:
questions.explanation: 5x divides both terms: 10x^2 divided by 5x is 2x and 15x divided by 5x is 3. A larger common factor such as 10x would not divide the second term.
questions.commonMistake: Taking 10x, which does not divide 15x into a whole number.

questions.explanation: a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2) with a = x and b = 2 gives (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4).
questions.commonMistake: Choosing (x - 2)(x^2 - 2x + 4), which is the wrong sign pattern for a difference of cubes.

questions.explanation: The factors must multiply to 12 and sum to 7. Both (3,4) and (2,6) multiply to 12, but only 3 + 4 = 7.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing (x + 2)(x + 6) because 2 x 6 = 12, forgetting to check the sum.

questions.prompt: Which pair of numbers multiplies to -12 and adds to 1?
questions.explanation: The two numbers must multiply to -12, so one is positive and one negative; and their sum must be 1, so the positive one is larger. 4 and -3 satisfy both, since 4 x -3 = -12 and 4 - 3 = 1.
questions.commonMistake: Testing only the product and not checking the sum; several pairs multiply to -12.

questions.explanation: The common factor is 4a, the lowest common multiple of 8a and 12a, with b appearing in both terms. Dividing gives 2a and -3b.
81x^2 = (9x)^2 and 49 = 7^2, so the difference-of-squares identity applies.
From a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2) with a = x and b = 2y, the second factor is x^2 - 2xy + 4y^2.
The lowest common multiple of 12x and 18x is 6x, since 12/6 = 2 and 18/6 = 3.
questions.commonMistake: Taking 3x, which is a common factor but not the largest, leaving unnecessary fractions.

questions.explanation: Both terms are perfect squares once the square roots are taken, so the difference-of-squares identity applies directly.

questions.prompt: Factorise x^2 + 7x + 12, showing the splitting of the middle term.
questions.explanation: The middle term is deliberately rewritten as 3x + 4x so that each group has a common bracket.
questions.commonMistake: Writing x^2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4) without justification; the marks are for showing the grouping.

questions.explanation: The constant is positive but the middle coefficient is negative, so both factors in the pair are negative.
Using a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2) with a = 3 and b = 2x, the second factor is 9 - 6x + 4x^2.

The identity is applied twice: first to the difference of fourth powers, then to the factor x^2 - 9y^2 which is itself a difference of squares. The factor x^2 + 9y^2 does not factorise over the integers.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping after the first step and leaving x^2 - 9y^2 un-factored.

questions.explanation: After removing 3, the pair must multiply to -5 and sum to -4: -5 and 1 fit.
questions.commonMistake: Attempting to split the middle term before taking out the common factor, which wastes time.

questions.prompt: Factorise a^2 + 5a + 6 and state what happens if the expression were a^2 + 5a + 7.
questions.answer: a^2 + 5a + 6 = (a + 2)(a + 3), since 2 + 3 = 5 and 2 x 3 = 6. For a^2 + 5a + 7 no such pair exists: the factor pairs of 7 are (1,7) with sums 8 and -8, neither of which is 5, so the expression does not factorise over the integers.
questions.explanation: Not every quadratic factorises. The pairs must be found and tested; if none works, the answer is stated honestly rather than forced.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming every quadratic factorises and searching until something is found.

questions.prompt: Factorise 2x^3 + 6x^2 - 8x - 24 by grouping and verify your answer.
questions.answer: Group as (2x^3 + 6x^2) - (8x + 24) = 2x^2(x + 3) - 8(x + 3) = (x + 3)(2x^2 - 8) = 2(x + 3)(x^2 - 4) = 2(x + 3)(x + 2)(x - 2). Verification at x = 2: the original gives 16 + 24 - 16 - 24 = 0 and the factorised form gives 2 x 5 x 4 x 0 = 0. At x = 1: original 2 + 6 - 8 - 24 = -24; factorised 2 x 4 x 3 x (-1) = -24.
questions.explanation: Grouping must be continued: after (x + 3) is taken out, the remaining bracket is itself a difference of squares.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at (x + 3)(2x^2 - 8) when the question asks for the complete factorisation.

questions.answer: x^3 + y^3 = (x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2), so the fraction is (x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2)/(x + y) = x^2 - xy + y^2, with the condition x + y is not zero.
questions.explanation: The cancellation is only valid because x^3 + y^3 has x + y as a genuine factor of the whole expression.
questions.commonMistake: Cancelling x with x and y with y separately, which is not legitimate here.

questions.answer: a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2), so the fraction is (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)/(a - b) = a^2 + ab + b^2, with a not equal to b.
questions.explanation: The difference-of-cubes identity supplies the factor a - b, which cancels with the denominator.

questions.prompt: Show that (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) simplifies to x + 1, and state the value of the expression when x = 1.
questions.answer: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1), so the fraction is (x - 1)(x + 1)/(x - 1) = x + 1 provided x is not 1. When x = 1 the original expression has zero in the denominator and is undefined; the simplified form gives x + 1 = 2, which is why the restriction must be stated.
questions.explanation: Simplifying a fraction never removes the restriction on the original denominator. This is examined regularly as a one-mark trap.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 2 for x = 1 and ignoring that the original fraction is undefined there.

questions.prompt: Find the value of k so that x^2 + kx + 15 has integer factors.
questions.answer: k can be 16, 8, -16 or -8, giving (x + 1)(x + 15), (x + 3)(x + 5), (x - 1)(x - 15) and (x - 3)(x - 5) respectively.
questions.explanation: Listing the factor pairs of the constant and computing their sums gives every possible k.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the positive values of k and omitting the negative pairings.

questions.answer: The first is (x - 2)(x - 3) since -2 + -3 = -5 and 2 x 3 = 6. The second is (x - 3)(x - 4) since -3 + -4 = -7 and 3 x 4 = 12. The product is therefore (x - 2)(x - 3)^2(x - 4).
questions.explanation: Factorising each bracket separately first is far quicker than attempting to multiply and then factorise the degree-four result.
questions.commonMistake: Missing that (x - 3) appears twice and writing it only once.

questions.prompt: Factorise 4x^2 - 12x + 9 and comment on the number of real roots of the equation 4x^2 - 12x + 9 = 0.
questions.answer: 4x^2 - 12x + 9 = (2x - 3)^2 = (2x - 3)(2x - 3). The equation therefore becomes (2x - 3)^2 = 0, so 2x - 3 = 0 and x = 3/2. There is exactly one real root, a repeated root, because a perfect square can only vanish when its base vanishes.
questions.explanation: A repeated factor gives a repeated root. This is the geometric meaning of the tangent of a parabola being a double root.
questions.commonMistake: Writing x = 3 and x = 1.5 as two separate solutions.

questions.prompt: Without expanding, find the value of 87 x 93.
questions.explanation: The two factors are of the form (a - b)(a + b), so a^2 - b^2 turns the product into a short calculation.
questions.commonMistake: Long multiplication, which is correct but slow under time pressure.

questions.prompt: A student factorises x^2 - 4 as (x - 2)^2. Identify the error and give the correct factorisation.
questions.answer: The student has confused a difference with a sum. (x - 2)^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4, which contains a middle term that x^2 - 4 does not have. The correct factorisation is (x - 2)(x + 2), from a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b). Checking: (x - 2)(x + 2) = x^2 + 2x - 2x - 4 = x^2 - 4.
questions.explanation: The error comes from applying the square identity to what is actually a difference of squares.
questions.commonMistake: Not checking by expanding the proposed factorisation, which would have shown the extra -4x + 4 immediately.

questions.explanation: The first term is the perfect square (xy)^2, so the identity applies with a = xy and b = 4.

questions.answer: Using a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b) with a = 2x + 3 and b = 2x - 3: the sum is 4x and the difference is 6, so the expression factorises as 4x x 6 = 24x.
questions.explanation: Recognising an expression of the form A - B where both A and B are squares, and using (a + b) and (a - b) directly.
questions.commonMistake: Expanding both squares first and collecting terms, which works but is slower.

questions.explanation: 5, a and b all divide every term, and the lowest common multiple is 5ab. The remaining bracket cannot be factorised further.
questions.commonMistake: Taking 15ab, which does not divide the first term.

questions.prompt: Explain why x^2 + 2x + 1 factors but x^2 + 2x + 2 does not, and give the complete factorisation of the first.
questions.answer: For x^2 + 2x + 1 the pair must multiply to 1 and sum to 2; the pair 1 and 1 does both, giving (x + 1)(x + 1) = (x + 1)^2. For x^2 + 2x + 2 the pair must multiply to 2 and sum to 2; the factor pairs of 2 are (1,2) and (-1,-2) with sums 3 and -3, neither of which is 2, so it does not factorise over the integers.
questions.explanation: The pair test is decisive and quick; there is no alternative factorisation for a monic quadratic.
questions.commonMistake: Writing (x + 2)^2 for x^2 + 2x + 2, which would give a middle term of 4x.

questions.answer: The numerator is (x - 2)^2, so the fraction is (x - 2)^2/(x - 2) = x - 2, valid provided x is not 2. When x = 2 the original expression is undefined, so the restriction must be carried through.
questions.explanation: A squared factor cancels one power of itself, leaving one factor behind; the value of the original expression at x = 2 is not defined.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 0 for x = 2 by substituting into the simplified form.
